title: Code block primitive — five interaction directions
brief: A CodeMirror-backed canvas code block should read like code, keep the canvas free for sketching, and expose language, font size, line numbers, and character-width control without turning a selected shape into a control panel.
defaultWhy: Selection ribbon + width popover wins because the everyday controls match the supplied LabVIEW-like toolbar while width gets the FigJam-like preset-and-custom chooser it deserves. It is immediate for the four frequent adjustments yet preserves the canvas as the primary surface.
decisionHinge: This recommendation depends on width being an occasional deliberate decision. If people change width as often as they change font size, V4’s always-visible header controls become the better default despite making the block busier.
invariants: The same Python function, 16 px font, visible line numbers, and 48-character width appear in every specimen.
Code is an editable canvas shape; moving, resizing, selection, undo, and persistence stay tldraw-owned.
CodeMirror owns text editing and language highlighting only; the whiteboard never infers program semantics.
boundary: These are browser-runnable interaction prototypes using representative code. The chosen production slice will use a real custom tldraw shape and CodeMirror; language services, execution, linting, and source projection are deliberately outside the primitive.

requirements.name: Fast selected-shape adjustment
requirements.why: Language, type scale, and line numbers are the direct editing controls shown in the reference and should not interrupt reading or sketching.
requirements.passCondition: With a code block selected, a person can see and change language, font size, and line-number visibility in one stable canvas state.

anchors.1: Requires opening a remote panel or remembering a command for ordinary settings.
anchors.3: The controls work but use space or steps that obscure the code.
anchors.5: All common adjustments are obvious, one click away, and do not conceal the selected code.

requirements.name: Character-width confidence
requirements.why: The requested width unit is meaningfully different from pixels: a reader needs a predictable line measure and feedback while dragging.
requirements.passCondition: The user can choose a common character width, type any valid character count, or drag the shape and see the same count.

anchors.1: Width is pixels-only or its relationship to code measure is hidden.
anchors.3: Character width is available but requires translation or lacks drag feedback.
anchors.5: Presets, exact entry, and live drag feedback all agree on one visible character count.

requirements.name: Readable code, quiet canvas
requirements.why: A code primitive is primarily read on a whiteboard; its editing chrome should recede when the work is not being configured.
requirements.passCondition: The unselected block is a calm code surface, while the selected state keeps controls outside the edited text and preserves its line measure.

anchors.1: Persistent chrome competes with code or hides content.
anchors.3: The block remains readable but selected controls feel crowded or disconnected.
anchors.5: Code stays the visual subject; controls appear only at the appropriate moment and are visually coherent.

requirements.name: Native tldraw fit
requirements.why: The product boundary requires a stock tldraw engine with custom shapes and components only, so the surface must make stock selection and resize behavior feel intentional.
requirements.passCondition: The concept has a clear custom-shape seam, uses tldraw selection/resize rather than reimplementing it, and does not introduce program inference.

anchors.1: Requires replacing canvas interaction or adds programming-language behavior.
anchors.3: Could be built as a custom shape but duplicates a stock interaction seam.
anchors.5: Uses a custom shape, stock selection/resize, a plain persisted prop model, and CodeMirror only for editing.

hardGates.name: Uses CodeMirror for code editing
hardGates.why: The requested editor must be the real implementation boundary, not a styled textarea or a rich-text approximation.

hardGates.name: Stock canvas interaction preserved
hardGates.why: The solution must use tldraw’s supported shape/tool/component seams and retain native drag, resize, selection, undo, and persistence.

hardGates.name: No implicit program semantics
hardGates.why: A code note may be incomplete or exploratory; it must not lint, execute, infer types, or become a second language.

variants.name: Selection ribbon
variants.thesis: A single floating strip puts every frequent formatting control directly above the selected code block; width changes begin with a compact character pill.
variants.bestWhen: The code shape is often formatted immediately after insertion and the toolbar should match the supplied LabVIEW reference.
variants.losesWhen: Many people need exact custom widths; its compact width pill hides the richer chooser one click too deep.

variants.name: Command surface
variants.thesis: The selected block stays pure code; a compact command menu makes each adjustment a searchable verb with typed numeric entry.
variants.bestWhen: Keyboard-oriented users value one command vocabulary across every canvas primitive and settings are infrequent.
variants.losesWhen: The reference’s visible, mouse-first toolbar is the expected discoverability model for a casual whiteboard session.

variants.name: Inline header
variants.thesis: The code shape owns a small header with its language, size, numbered-lines switch, and character width always in view.
variants.bestWhen: A board is a static documentation artifact and each code block should explain its own display choices without selection.
variants.losesWhen: Canvas density and a clean unselected reading state matter more than always-visible metadata.

variants.name: Ribbon + width popover
variants.thesis: Use a clean selected-object ribbon for language, font size, and line numbers, then give the width chip a focused FigJam-like popover: named character presets, custom number entry, and live drag feedback.
variants.bestWhen: People want fast visual controls for common formatting plus a confident character-based width decision when layout matters.
variants.losesWhen: Width must be edited continually on many blocks; then the extra popover becomes needless ceremony.
